title: The Curator's Spheres
summary: Probe sealed spheres with charged rods, watch how they swing, and deduce which are positive, negative or neutral.
subject: physics
concepts: Repulsion as the test of charge
learningOutcome: After winning, the student can plan probes to find unknown charges, knows attraction proves little (neutral bodies are pulled too) but repulsion proves like charges, and uses the rubbing convention.

levels.title: Three sealed spheres
levels.adds: Baseline: one positive, one negative and one neutral sphere. Probe them with a + rod and a − rod.
hints: Drag a rod close to a sphere and watch which way it swings.
Like charges repel and unlike attract. A push is the only result that proves anything.
A sphere pulled toward a + rod is negative or neutral. Try the − rod on it: a negative sphere will be pushed away.

levels.title: Who is neutral?
levels.adds: New idea: neutral spheres exist and the counts are unknown. Attraction can fool you, so look for a sphere pulled by BOTH rods.
hints: Every reaction looks equally strong, so only the direction carries information.
A neutral body is attracted by a charged rod of either sign.
A sphere attracted by the + rod AND by the − rod must be neutral. A charged sphere is pushed away by one of the rods.

levels.title: Glass and plastic
levels.adds: New idea: the rods are labelled by material, not sign. Use the rubbing convention to know which is which.
hints: Recall which charge a glass rod gets when rubbed with silk, and which a plastic rod gets when rubbed with fur.
Glass rubbed with silk is positive; plastic rubbed with fur is negative.
Once you know each rod's sign, probe every sphere with both and apply the repulsion test.

levels.title: Mystery rods
levels.adds: New idea: you do not even know your rods' signs. Calibrate them on a reference sphere first, then identify the spheres and rod X.
hints: One rod is positive and the other negative, but you do not know which.
The reference sphere is known to be positive. A rod it pushes away is positive too.
Once you know which rod is which, treat them like the + and − rods from level 1.

misconceptions: Attraction proves the bodies have opposite charges (a neutral body is attracted too)
A neutral body can't be affected by a charged one
The sign convention is arbitrary per experiment
